column1: What runtime information does an actual SQL Server execution plan add to the compiled plan?
column2:
Runtime information, such as actual row counts and execution warnings.
The optimizer supplies estimates before execution. The actual plan adds measurements from this run, such as actual rows, plus runtime warnings. Capturing it runs the statement, including any data changes.
Review source

column1: Which execution plan operator locates rows through nonclustered index key values or ranges?
column2:
Index Seek.
An Index Seek uses an index key to locate a value or range rather than reading the entire index. A wide range can still touch many pages, so the operator name alone does not establish efficiency.
Review source

column1: When can a table or index scan be an efficient access method?
column2:
When the table is small or the query needs many rows.
A scan can read the needed pages more cheaply than many separate lookups. For example, a query that returns nearly every row often gains little from looking up rows one at a time.
Review source

column1: What does a large gap between estimated and actual rows suggest about the optimizer's prediction?
column2:
A cardinality estimation problem: the optimizer misjudged how many rows the operation would process.
The estimated row count is the optimizer's prediction. A large gap can lead it to choose an unsuitable join or memory grant. Stale statistics are one possible cause, not proof.
Review source

column1: Which command refreshes existing statistics that no longer represent a table's data distribution?
column2:
UPDATE STATISTICS.
Statistics describe the distribution of column values. Refreshing existing statistics gives the optimizer newer information for estimating how many rows a filter returns. It does not automatically create every missing statistic.
Review source

column1: Why does SQL Server perform a Key Lookup after reading a nonclustered index on a clustered table?
column2:
The nonclustered index lacks columns that the query needs.
For example, the index can locate an order by CustomerID but lack its OrderDate. A Key Lookup fetches the missing value from the clustered index, potentially once for each matching row.
Review source

column1: How can a nonclustered index cover missing output columns and avoid Key Lookups?
column2:
Add the needed output columns as included columns.
Included columns are stored at the leaf level of a nonclustered index without becoming search keys. Adding the missing output columns can avoid trips to the clustered index but makes the index larger.
Review source

column1: What does a Sort or Hash spill warning indicate?
column2:
The operator wrote intermediate results to tempdb because its working memory was insufficient.
The operator could not finish all of its work in the memory available to it, so it used tempdb for intermediate data. Compare actual rows and memory grant details before choosing a fix.
Review source

column1: Why can a query that reserves more workspace memory than it uses make other queries wait?
column2:
It reserves memory that other queries need.
A memory grant reserves workspace for operations such as sorts and hash joins. If a query reserves far more than it uses, other queries can wait for memory even when that reservation is mostly unused.
Review source

column1: What missing condition can explain a No Join Predicate warning in a SQL Server execution plan?
column2:
A missing join condition that produces a Cartesian product.
A Cartesian product pairs every row from one input with every row from the other. That can be intentional, but an omitted join condition can accidentally multiply the work and produce wrong results.
Review source

column1: How can comparing an indexed column with a parameter of a different type hurt index access?
column2:
An implicit conversion on the indexed column can prevent an efficient seek.
If SQL Server converts the indexed column for comparison, it can lose an efficient way to search that key. A conversion of the input value does not necessarily have the same effect.
Review source

column1: What must you assess before implementing a missing-index suggestion?
column2:
Its benefit and cost across the workload, including existing indexes and write overhead.
The optimizer estimates the value of the index for particular queries. Compare the recommendation with current indexes and measure read improvements against extra storage and the work of maintaining it during writes.
Review source

column1: Which dynamic management view reports aggregate statistics for completed executions of cached query statements?
column2:
sys.dm_exec_query_stats.
A dynamic management view (DMV) exposes engine state. This DMV totals measurements such as CPU and reads for completed executions of statements whose plans remain cached, not requests currently in progress.
Review source

column1: What happens to sys.dm_exec_query_stats rows when their plan leaves the cache?
column2:
The corresponding rows disappear.
The statistics belong to the cached plan entry. If the engine evicts the plan, those totals go away with it. Use Query Store when you need retained history beyond the plan cache.
Review source

column1: Why consider execution count as well as average CPU when prioritizing query tuning?
column2:
A frequently executed moderate-cost query can consume more CPU overall.
Average CPU is the cost of one execution. A query that uses 5 milliseconds of CPU and runs 1,000 times uses more total CPU than one that uses 100 milliseconds and runs twice.
Review source

column1: Which dynamic management view shows currently executing requests and their waits?
column2:
sys.dm_exec_requests.
A request is work currently submitted to the engine. This view can show what that work is waiting for and which session blocks it, but the platform and permissions determine which requests you can see.
Review source

column1: Which dynamic management view identifies authenticated sessions and their client applications?
column2:
sys.dm_exec_sessions.
A session represents a database connection and can exist even when it runs no request. The session view lists attributes such as the login and reported client program, which give context to a visible request.
Review source

column1: Which dynamic management view reports individual tasks waiting on resources?
column2:
sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks.
A task is a unit of execution work. A parallel request can have multiple tasks, and one task can wait for a different resource than another task in the same request.
Review source

column1: Which missing-index DMV lists the table and suggested equality, inequality, and included columns?
column2:
sys.dm_db_missing_index_details.
Equality columns are proposed for exact matches, inequality columns for other comparisons, and included columns for additional data needed by the query. These are suggestions rather than a complete index design.
Review source

column1: Which DMV reports how often missing-index groups are needed and their estimated benefit?
column2:
sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats.
The view reports how often queries can benefit from a missing-index group and what the optimizer estimates the benefit to be. It does not measure a speedup for an index that does not exist.
Review source

column1: What happens to missing-index DMV suggestions after an instance restart?
column2:
They are cleared.
These suggestions live in memory and disappear when the instance restarts. An empty view immediately after a restart does not prove that the workload has no useful indexing opportunities.
Review source

column1: Which database permission permits sys.dm_exec_query_stats access on an Azure SQL Standard S2 single database?
column2:
VIEW DATABASE STATE.
Standard S2 is the context for this permission. It grants visibility to database performance information in that database. Lower service objectives and elastic pools have distinct permission requirements for this DMV.
Review source

column1: Which server permission does sys.dm_exec_query_stats require in SQL Server 2025?
column2:
VIEW SERVER PERFORMANCE STATE.
This is a server-level permission for accessing the DMV in SQL Server 2022 and later. It differs from database-level permissions used for some Azure SQL Database service objectives.
Review source

column1: Which Fabric SQL database tool displays performance metrics and query-level details?
column2:
The Performance Dashboard.
Open Performance summary from the Fabric SQL query editor to see database metrics and query details. Use it to narrow down query performance issues, rather than to measure all Fabric capacity consumption.
Review source

column1: Which Fabric app shows SQL database capacity consumption, including user-generated and system-generated T-SQL work?
column2:
The Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app.
The Capacity Metrics app includes work done by users and the service. It answers a capacity question, so its totals need not match a dashboard chart limited to user-query CPU.
Review source

column1: Which workload contributes CPU to the Fabric SQL database Performance Dashboard's CPU trend chart?
column2:
User queries only.
The dashboard's CPU trend describes queries submitted by users. It excludes background maintenance and provisioning. Use capacity metrics to investigate consumption that is absent from the user-query trend.
Review source
